'''''Lithospermum erythrorhizon''''', commonly called '''purple gromwell''', '''red stoneroot''', '''red gromwell''', '''red-root gromwell''' and '''redroot lithospermum''', is a plant species in the family [[Boraginaceae]].<ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN}}</ref> It is called ''zǐcǎo'' ({{lang|zh|紫草}}) in Chinese, {{lang|ko-Latn|jichi}} ({{lang|ko|지치}}) in Korean, and {{lang|ja-Latn|murasaki}} ({{lang|ja-Hrkt|ムラサキ}}; {{lang|ja-Hani|茈}}, {{Lang|ja|紫}}) in Japanese.<ref name="GRIN" />

The dried root of ''Lithospermum erythrorhizon'' (lithospermum root or ''Lithospermi Radix'') is a [[Traditional Chinese medicine|Chinese herbal medicine]] with various antiviral and biological activities, including inhibition of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1).<ref>Chen, X., et al. (2003). [http://aac.asm.org/content/47/9/2810.long Shikonin, a component of Chinese herbal medicine, inhibits chemokine receptor function and suppresses human immunodeficiency virus type 1.] ''Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy'' 47(9), 2810-16.</ref><ref>Gao, H., et al. (2011). Anti-adenovirus activities of shikonin, a component of Chinese herbal medicine in vitro. ''Biol Pharm Bull''. 34(2) 197-202.</ref>

The genome of ''Lithospermum erythrorhizon'' has been sequenced and has facilitated the discovery of a putative retrotransposition-derived duplication event that produced a [[4-hydroxybenzoate geranyltransferase]] gene involved in [[alkannin]] biosynthesis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Auber|first1=Robert P.|last2=Suttiyut|first2=Thiti|last3=McCoy|first3=Rachel M.|last4=Ghaste|first4=Manoj|last5=Crook|first5=Joseph W.|last6=Pendleton|first6=Amanda L.|last7=Widhalm|first7=Joshua R.|last8=Wisecaver|first8=Jennifer H.|display-authors=3|date=2020-06-01|title=Hybrid de novo genome assembly of red gromwell (''Lithospermum erythrorhizon'') reveals evolutionary insight into shikonin biosynthesis|journal=Horticulture Research|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|page=82 |doi=10.1038/s41438-020-0301-9|pmid=32528694 |pmc=7261806|bibcode=2020HorR....7...82A }}</ref>

== Biochemistry ==
The enzyme [[4-hydroxybenzoate geranyltransferase]] utilizes [[Geranyl pyrophosphate|geranyl diphosphate]] and [[4-hydroxybenzoate]] to produce [[3-geranyl-4-hydroxybenzoate]] and diphosphate. Biosynthetically, [[alkannin]] is produced in plants from the intermediates 4-hydroxybenzoic acid and [[geranyl pyrophosphate]]. This enzyme is involved in [[alkannin|shikonin]] biosynthesis.

The enzyme [[geranylhydroquinone 3''-hydroxylase]] uses [[geranylhydroquinone]], NADPH, H<sup>+</sup> and O<sub>2</sub> to produce [[3-hydroxygeranylhydroquinone]], NADP<sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O.

==Uses==
It has been cultivated in [[Japan]] since the [[Nara period]] for its [[root]], which can be used for [[herbal medicine]] and to make [[dyes]].<ref>Dalby, Liza (2001). ''Kimono: Fashioning Culture''. University of Washington Press, pp. 236–237. {{ISBN|0-295-98155-5}}.</ref><ref>Wada Yoshiko; Mary Kellogg Rice, and Jane Barton (1983). ''Shibori: The Inventive Art of Japanese Shaped Resist Dyeing''. Kodansha, pp. 278–279. {{ISBN|0-87011-559-6}}.</ref>

Before the introduction of [[mauvine|synthetic dyes]] to [[Meiji period]] Japan, the roots were commonly used as a dyestuff for luxury textiles, typically high-end [[kimono]] and {{transliteration|ja|[[obi (sash)|obi]]}}. The process of extracting purple dyestuff from the roots was an exceedingly long, complex and time-consuming process, necessitating its relatively high expense:

{{blockquote|The roots [of the plant] are collected and dried for two to three months to mature the color. While this occurs, the silk is pre-[[mordant]]ed [...] the mordanting process involves repeated immersion of the cloth or yarn in the alum bath and drying over a two- or three-month period. To prepare the dyestuff, the gromwell roots are softened overnight in 60° [Celsius] water and then pounded to release the dye. The silk is then repeatedly immersed in the bath, aired to allow more oxygen to penetrate the cloth and then steeped in the dye until the desired color is achieved. When the dyeing is completed the cloth is placed in dark storage for as long as a year while the color continues to mature.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1473&context=tsaconf |title=The Impact of Synthetic Dyes on the Luxury Textiles of Meiji Japan |last=Parmal |first=Pamela A. |year=2004 |publisher=Textile Society of America |type=Symposium Proceedings (474) |format=pdf |access-date=21 August 2020 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200721104553/https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1473&context=tsaconf |archive-date=21 July 2020}}</ref>}}

For a deep purple, up to 50 dips could be needed. {{transliteration|ja|Shikonzome}} dye loses colour remarkably fast, literally as the fibers are being dipped, meaning it was often used for {{transliteration|ja|bokashi}} ([[ombré]]) dying, and the resulting colour was varied and uneven, with each strand a slightly different shade.<ref name="mochi_furisode">{{cite web |title=Kimono Mochi: private kimono collection photographs and text |url=https://kimonomochi.jimdofree.com/ |website=kimonomochi kimono collection |access-date=31 July 2021}}</ref>

One [[Japanese language|Japanese word]] for the plant, {{Nihongo|2=紫|3=murasaki}}, inspired the [[pen name]] "[[Lady Murasaki]]" for the author of ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'' and is also the source of the general Japanese term for the color [[purple]], {{Nihongo|2=紫色|3=murasaki iro}}.<ref>{{Citation|title=Things to Wear — A History of Japanese Clothing: Japanese Dyestuffs|url=http://www.reconstructinghistory.com/japanese/dyes.html|year=2003|last1=McGann|first1=Kass|accessdate=2007-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070221031030/http://www.reconstructinghistory.com/japanese/dyes.html|archive-date=21 Feb 2007}}</ref> Additional terms were used for specific shades of purple within this range, particularly during the [[Heian period]]; names such as {{transliteration|ja|usuki murasaki}} ("pale purple") and {{transliteration|ja|asaki murasaki}} ("light purple") formed important distinctions when dressing in [[jūnihitoe|specifically-layered clothing]], and could also indicate (typically high) rank.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://sengokudaimyo.com/garb/kasane-no-irome |title=Kasane no Irome |last=Bryant |first=Anthony J. |publisher=Sengoku Daimyo |access-date=21 August 2020 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200821103838/https://sengokudaimyo.com/garb/kasane-no-irome |archive-date=21 August 2020 }}</ref>

The dyes made from its root also had other names, such as ''shikon'' (紫根) {{Nihongo|2=紫根|3=shikon}},<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/m/murasaki.htm |title= JAANUS / Murasaki 紫|website=www.aisf.or.jp |access-date=2007-04-20}}{{title missing|date=September 2022}}</ref> but all of them were difficult to work with because of their requirement for an [[alum]]-rich [[mordant]] and the resulting colors' extreme vulnerability to [[photobleaching]]. During the [[Heian Period]], [[sumptuary]] laws restricted ''murasaki''-dyed clothing to the [[Empress]] and her [[ladies in waiting]].
